Notes: Operating_System- Process Management

Process Management
​​​​​​​​​​​​​Currently we use multiprocessing ,multithreading systems. Initially the systems were single programming OS where in there were limitations on processing speed and capabilities. An idea to create small processes and then the threads increased the processing speed to much greater extent. In this chapter we are going to study concepts of process, thread, how a process and threads are created, scheduling of processes etc. in short how an OS manages the process. Process managment is one of the major importang function of OS. 
Concept of process
In a computer system , complete program is never executed at a time. The program is divided into parts internally by the system and then these small parts are executed separately. So in short we can say that,
  1. Program is a passive entity.
  2. Process is a active entity.
Hence we can define Process as "Program in execution."
So, a Process is a part of program which is under execution. Any program or process which is executed by the system is to be brought into the primary memory(RAM).

Let us understand memory structure used by any C or Java code. The Primary Memory (Main Memory or RAM) is virtually divided in some parts. Shown below is a diagrammatic representation of Memory Allocation.
​
Stack :: The Stack contains the temporary data such as method/function, parameters, return address and local variables.

Data  :: This section contains the global and static variables.

Text   :: This includes the current activity represented by the value of Program Counter and the contents of the processor's registers.

Heap :: This is dynamically allocated memory to a process during its run time. This memory can be released once execution is completed.
Process Life Cycle (Process State)  
When  a process executes it passes throudh differen states . Following is the diagram showing life cycle of a  process.

​
Detailed diagram of process life cycle  

​
Every process falls under one of the following state.
1. New            -Newly created process.
2. Ready         -Process in ready queue waiting for CPU.
3. Running     -Process under execution.
4. Terminate  -Logical end of process.
5. Wait            -The process is waiting for some event to occur (such as the completion
                         of an I/O operation)
                           
Let us get some more information about  the states of process (Process life cycle).
1. New           
    Process is in New State means a new process is created , and it is yet not active. So newly created process is
    said to be in new state.
2. Ready 
    Process comes in RAM and gets placed in a Queue. This queue is called as Ready Queue. The process is said
    to  be in the ready state, if process is in ready queue and is waiting for CPU. This task of bringing process from
    job queue to ready queue is done by long term scheduler.
3. Running
     Process in RAM gets CPU for execution. This task of dispatching process from Ready Queue to CPU is done by
     short term scheduler also called as Dispatcher.  This process is in the running state.
4. Terminate      
     Process is completed logically. Hence process is terminated. Now system has no record of this process.
5. Wait / Block
    Sometimes when process is in execution phase, it may require some other resources to complete  the
    execution (mostly these are i/o resources. Speed of i/o resources is very slow hence CPU becomes ideal). 
    System puts this process in the wait state and CPU starts executing another process. Once i/o operation of            process is completed, process again goes in Ready Queue and waits for CPU.
6. Suspend ready
    Sometimes if the number of processes is very large, than all the processes cannot be accommodated in the          ready queue . Hence, some processes are moved  to secondary storage device. This state is called as   
    suspended ready state.  Once when there is enough space in the ready queue, the processes from secondaty
    storage device are brought back in ready queue.
7. Suspend wait or suspend blocked
    This is similar to ready suspended. The processes in blocked suspended state are in secondary memory. 
    These processes are initially in the blocked/wait state in main memory waiting for some event. If this memory
    becomes insufficient,  these processes are suspended and are placed in the secondary memory. A process
    may go from blocked suspended to ready suspended if its work is done.​​​​​​​   

 Process Control Block (PCB)    
Process Control Block (PCB) is a simple data structure maintained by the system. This PCB stores detailed information about a Process . Every process has it's separate PCB.  The information of the Process is used by  CPU at the Run time . PCB is also called as Task Control Block. The PCB is identified by an unique integer called as Process ID (PID). System also maintains a table of all these PCBs , to keep track of all running processes.   ​

Process goes in terminate state. It's entry from PCB is deleted.   
When OS has a timer interrupt ,it saves the state of currently running process & reloads the state of next process to be executed.
--This action of saving state & reloading the state actively in switching is known as a context switching.
--Context Switching involves, storing the context or state of a process so that it can be reloaded when required and execution can be resumed from the same point as earlier.
--This is a feature of a multitasking operating system and allows a single CPU to be shared by multiple processes.

Types of Processes  
1. I/O bound process   :: spends more time doing I/O than computations.
2. CPU bound process :: spends more time doing computations than I/O.  

Note :: Every process in the memory has it's own PCB. Entries of all these PCBs are maintained in a data structure called as Process Control Table. System gets an information about all the running processes through this Process Control Table. When any process terminates , it's entry is deleted from Process Control Table.

Long term scheduler picks up the proper combination of I/O bound processes and CPU bound processes. This is called as Load-Balancing. Load-Balancing is done to achieve optimum utilization of CPU.     
Schedulers in OS
Scheduler Concept
Scheduler is a s/w program of operating system which schedules the processes.
Schedulers are of 3 types.  

1. Long Term Scheduler 
This code of OS takes the process from the Job Queue to Ready Queue. When a new process is created it enters Job Queue. Process in the Job Queue waits to be taken to Ready Queue. Depending on the load in Ready Queue, Long Term Scheduler takes the process from Job Queue to Ready Queue.

2. Short Term Scheduler 
This code of OS picks the process from ready queue and assigns it to CPU for execution. Short term scheduler is also called as Dispatcher. Process in the Ready Queue is ready to get executed and waits for it's turn. When CUP completes it's current task , a process from Ready Queue is dispatched to CPU. This task is done by the Dispatcher  ( Short Term Scheduler ).

3. Medium Term Schedule  (mid term scheduler)
Sometimes Ready Queue gets overloaded by processes . At this point of time Med Term scheduler creates a Swap Area on the hard disk of the system and moves some processes on the disk .This technique of moving processes from RAM to hard disk is called as Swap-Out. After Ready Queue gets lighter load ,the processes  are moved back again ot RAM. This is called as Swap-In technique.
Medium Term Scheduler will come into picture only when Ready Queue gets loaded with too many processes.
Degree of Multiprogramming  
Number of processes in the Ready Queue actively waiting for CPU defines the degree of multiprogramming. More the degree of multiprogramming , more is the load on short term scheduler but CPU utilization is optimum in that case.
Process creation and termination

​
Process Creation 
  •  Process creation is system call to the kernel.
  •  fork() command in linux is used to create a new process.
  •  When the system starts(boots) ,'init' is the first process created by OS. It has pid=1 .
  •  This process is father of all  the processes created there after.
  •  In Unix-like systems(i.e Unix,Linux,MacOS) father process is termed as systemd.
  •  This process is the last to terminate.
  •  kill() function is used to terminate the process.     
Process Termation 
Whenever  any process  terminats, it follows certain steps
  •      It returns delivery status to parent process.
  •      It releases all the resources which it was holding .
  •      It deletes its PCB from Process Control Table. 

  1. Cascading Effect 
  •       Sometimes parent processes is terminated irrespective of running child processes.  In such cases child                processes are forcefully terminated.
  •       So all the processes running under parent are terminated.
  •       This is called as cascading effect.

  2. Orphan Process 
  •       Sometimes if parent process is terminated, and child processes still remains, it is called as Orphan Process.
  •       In this case, the orphan processes are assigned to main 'init' process.

  3. Zombie Process 
  •       Sometimes though the process terminates , it's PCB remains in the memory.
          This is called as Zombi process.  

Functions to manage processes

  • fork() function
fork() is a system call used to create a new process. This new process created by fork() is called a child 
process, while the process that calls fork() is referred to as the parent process. This is a critical mechanism in
Unix-like operating systems (including Linux) for process creation.
When a process calls fork(), the operating system creates a new process. This new process is a duplicate of the
calling process, but it has its unique process identifier (PID).
The fork() system call returns two different values 
For the parent process, it returns the PID of the newly created child process.
For the child process, it returns 0.
If there’s an error in creating the child process, fork() returns -1 to the parent process.
 
 After a fork() call, both the parent and child processes continue executing from the point where fork() was called. Proper synchronization between the two processes is often necessary to prevent issues such as race conditions.
Processes created can themselves create more processes, forming a tree-like structure of processes. Each child can also execute a different program using the exec() family of functions after a fork() call. 
Example:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    pid_t pid = fork(); // Create a new process

    if (pid < 0) {
        // Error handling for fork failure
        perror("fork failed");
        return 1;
    } else if (pid == 0) {
        // This block is executed by the child process
        printf("Child process: My PID is %d\n", getpid());
    } else {
        // This block is executed by the parent process
        printf("Parent process: Created child process with PID %d\n", pid);
    }

    return 0;
}​​​​​​​
  • wait() function
Function wait() suspends the parent process until a child process is running. The wait() call returns the 
process ID (PID) of the terminated child process. If there are no child processes running when the wait() call is
made, it has no effect.
  • exit() function
Function exit() causes a waiting parent process to resume execution. The exit() call takes a parameter value,
status  and returns it to the parent process. 
  • kill() function   
In operating systems, the kill() system call is used to send signals to processes. The most common use of kill() is to terminate a process, but it can also be used to send various other signals that can instruct a process to perform different actions.
Signature of the kill() function in C is 
  int kill(pid_t pid, int sig);
Here, pid is the process identifier of the target process, and sig is the signal number that you want to send.
Zombie Process :
If a child process finishes executing but its parent hasn’t read its exit status, it becomes a "zombie" process. The parent can use the `wait()` system call to prevent this.
Process States : After forking, the parent and child can run concurrently, and their states can change based on CPU scheduling.
Process Synchronization
​​​​​Processes are either
   1. Cooperative  
       Gets affected by each other.
   2. Independent  
       Run individually and independently.

In the situation , where process is independent, other processes are not affected. This independent process nither shares data nor resources and works on it's own. But when the processes are co-operative , they affect each other in multiple ways, since they share data or resources etc.

Process synchronization  is a technique which is used to coordinate the process that uses the Shared Data. Process Synchronization means sharing system resources by processes in a such away that, concurrent access to shared data is handled, there by minimizing the chance of inconsistent data. Synchronization mechanism allow the processes to access critical section in a synchronized manner to avoid the inconsistent results.

Race Condition in OS
​
The condition where several processes try to access the resources and modify the shared data concurrently (simultaneously) . Outcome of the process depends on the particular order of execution that leads to data  inconsistency, this condition is called  as Race Condition. This condition can be avoided using the technique called Process Synchronization .

Critical Section 

​
Critical section is a section of the program where a process access the shared resources during its execution causing a race condition . To avoid race condition among the processes, we need to assure that only one process at a time can execute within the critical section.That resource may be any resource in a computer like a memory location, Data structure, CPU or any IO device. It means that in a group of cooperating processes, at a given point of time, only one process must be executing its critical section. If any other process also wants to execute its critical section, it must wait until the first one finishes.

For every critical section in the program, a synchronization mechanism adds
An entry section before the critical section
An exit section after the critical section

To achive process synchronization, OS uses synchronization tool. It is called as semaphore.  There are two types of semaphores
1. Binary Semaphore 
 It takes value 0 or 1.
 It is a special form of semaphore used for implementing mutual exclusion, hence it is often called a Mutex.
A binary semaphore is initialized to 1 and takes the values 0 and 1 during execution of program.
In Binary Semaphore, only two processes can compete to enter into its CRITICAL SECTION at any point in time, apart from this ,the condition of mutual exclusion is also preserved.
2. Counting Semaphore 
It works with many processes. It is used when there are multiple instances of one resource. It ensures that all the resources are allocated properly.
In counting semaphore, more than two processes can compete to enter into its CRITICAL SECTION at any point of time apart from this the condition of mutual exclusion is also preserved.

Classical Problems in Process Synchronization  
1.  Producer-Consumer Problem (Bounded Buffer Problem) 

​
The Producer-Consumer problem is a classical multi-process synchronization problem. Here we are trying to achive synchronization between more than one process. In the Producer-Consumer problem, Producer is producing some items, whereas there is one Consumer that is consuming the items produced by the Producer. The same memory buffer is shared by both producers and consumers which is of fixed-size. The task of the Producer is to produce the item, put it into the memory buffer, and again start producing new items. Where as the task of the Consumer is to consume the item from the memory buffer.
Below are a few points that are considered as the problems occurring  in Producer-Consumer:
--The producer should produce data only when the buffer is not full.
--In case it is found that the buffer is full, the producer is not allowed to store any data into the memory buffer.
--Data can only be consumed by the consumer if and only if the memory buffer is not empty.
--In case it is found that the buffer is empty, the consumer is not allowed to use any data from the
   memory buffer.
--Accessing memory buffer should not be allowed to producer and consumer at the same time.

The above problems of Producer and Consumer which occurred due to context switch and producing inconsistent result can be solved with the help of semaphores.
To solve the problem occurred above of race condition, we are going to use Binary Semaphore and Counting Semaphore.                                                                                                                                          

 
2. Reader/Writer Problem 

​
Consider that there are multiple processes accessing the shared resource.  Processes are of two types. They are reader and writer. Any number of readers can read from the shared resource simultaneously, but only one writer can write to the shared resource. When a writer is writing data to the resource, no other process can access the resource. A writer cannot write to the resource if there are non zero number of readers accessing the resource at that  time
The Solution 
From the above problem statement, it is evident that readers have higher priority than writer. If a writer wants to write to the resource, it must wait until there are no readers currently accessing that resource.
Here, we use one mutex m and a semaphore w. An integer variable read_count is used to maintain the number of readers currently accessing the resource. The variable read_count is initialized to 0. A value of 1 is given initially to m and w. Instead of having the process to acquire lock on the shared resource, we use the mutex m to make the process to acquire and release lock whenever it is updating the read_count variable.

The code for the writer process looks like this:
while(TRUE)
{
    wait(w);
    
   /* perform the write operation */
   
   signal(w); 
}
while(TRUE)
{
    //acquire lock
    wait(m);
    read_count++;
    if(read_count == 1)
        wait(w);
    
    //release lock  
    signal(m);  
/* perform the reading operation */    
    
    // acquire lock
    wait(m);   
    read_count--;
    if(read_count == 0)
        signal(w);
        
    // release lock
    signal(m);  
}
Deadlock in OS
Preemptive / NonPreemptive Processes
Process can be pre-emptive or non pre-emptive depending on how CPU executes it.

Preemptive: CPU can stop the execution of current process and can take other process for execution. This is called as preemption. In this case current status of the process is maintained so that CPU can exectue it further. Context Switching is done in this case to maintain the process status. This technique is used in time sharing systems. CPU will execute more processes in the given time. There is a switch overhead.          
               
Processes will preempt in 3 conditions--
   1. Process Terminates.
   2. Process goes in wait state.
   3. Time Quantum ends
      
NonPreemptive: Process executes till end or until it goes in a wait state. There is no switching overhead. Cannot be used in time sharing systems. Comparatively less processes will be executed in the given time.

Processor will switch to another process in 2 conditions
   1. Process Terminates.
   2. Process goes in wait state.

A process in operating systems uses different resources . Process always follows a certain method while accessing any system resource.
1) Request a resource 
While in execution, a process may require a resource to complete it's task. In that case , process will make a request of  resource to the system. Process will not grab the resource, but will wait if resource is not available. 
2) Use the resource 
Process will use the resource to complete the task.
3) Releases the resource.
After the task is completed, process will release the resource and will not hold it.

Deadlocks are a set of blocked processes each holding a resource and waiting to acquire a resource held by another process.
Deadlocks can be avoided by avoiding at least one of the four conditions.

​

All four conditions must be satisfied simultaneously for a  deadlock to occure.

1. Mutual Exclusion 
Resources shared (e.g read-only files) do not lead to deadlocks but resources, such as printers and tape drives, require exclusive access by a single process.
A resource should be held by only one process at a time.

 2. Hold and Wait 
 A process can hold multiple resources and still request more resources from other processes which are
 holding them.

3. No Pre-emption 
A resource cannot be preempted from a process by force. A process can only release a resource voluntarily.  
Deadlock arises due to the fact that a process can't be stopped once it starts. But, if we take the resource
away from the process which is causing deadlock then we can prevent deadlock. This is not a good approach
at all since if we take a resource away which is being used by the process then all the work which it has done
till now can become inconsistent.
 
4. Circular Wait 
A process is waiting for the resource held by the second process, which is waiting for the resource held by
the third process and so on, till the last process is waiting for a resource held by the first process. This forms a
circular chain.

All these 4 conditions must be necessarily satisfied for  the deadlock to occur.
In case of failure of any condition,  deadlock will not occur or will be rolled-back.
Handling Deadlock  
The above points focus on preventing deadlocks. But what to do once a deadlock has occurred.  Following three strategies can be used to remove deadlock after its occurrence.
1. Preemption 
We can take a resource from one process and give it to other.
This will resolve the deadlock situation, but sometimes it does cause a  problem.
2. Rollback Algorithm
In situations where deadlock is a real possibility, the system can periodically make a record of the state of each process and when deadlock occurs, roll everything back to the last checkpoint, and restart, but allocating resources differently so that deadlock does not occur. 
3. Kill one or more processes 
This is the simplest way, but it works.  If system remains in the state of deadlock after one process is killed,
then multiple processes will be killed one by one till system comes out of deadlock situation.
4. Deadlock Avoidance and prevention Algorithm (Banker's Algorithm)
Banker's Algorithm is called a resource allocation and deadlock avoidance algorithm . This Algorithm checks for the safe state. System will go in the deadlock situation if it requests any resource which is already allocated.  Algorithm checks if system will remain in safe state after allocating any resource.
Algorithm given by Banker needs following inputs::
  •         Max need of resources by each process.
  •         Currently allocated resources to each process.
  •         Max free available resources in the system.
​​​​​​​The request will only be granted under the below condition:   
     1. If the request made by the process is less than or equal to max need to  that process.
     2. If the request made by the process is less than or equal to the freely available resource in the
         system.       
Multiprocessing OS
Multiprocessing Systems are currently used in market . To increase the system throughput and use CPU to optimum level , entire OS s/w kept on evolving time to time. Multiprocessing system is a major achievement in this evolution , where the concept of implementation of multiple processors was practically used. Multiprocessing Systems broadly fall into two types--
1. Asymmetric Multiprocessing Systems 

​
In Asymmetric system one of the available processor is treated as a Master and other processors are called as Slaves. This Master handles all the OS privileged tasks. Slaves hand over OS related tasks to Master. This system was called as Master-Slave in the past. Now a days same architecture is referred to as a Client-Server.
Client talks to server if the processes to be executed are not within it's scope.

2. Symmetric Multiprocessing Systems     

​
In Symmetric system , no such division of task is done. All processors handle user-level processes as well as OS-level processes.  
Scheduling of processes in Multiprocessing system 
     --Ready Queue is maintained for each processor separately.
     --This helps in effective utilization of all the processors in the system.
     --Sometimes if one of the ready queue is overloaded with processes, some processes are moved to other              ready queue with  less load.
     --This is called as Push Migration technique.
     --Sometimes OS pulls the process from heavily loaded queue, this is called Pull Migration.
     --The technique of maintaining roughly same number of processes in all the ready queues is called as Load            Balancing.
     --A small program 'Task' keeps on running at the back end constantly to ensure  the load of Ready Queues.

​

Scheduling concepts   
​​​​​​​Important  scheduling Terminologies  
Jobs : It is a type of program without any kind of user interaction
Throughput :  Number of processes completed in the given unit of  time.
Multiprogramming  :  A number of programs are brought in memory at the same time.
Burst Time/Execution Time :  It is a time required by the process to complete execution. It is also called
                                                      running time.
Arrival Time : The time at which the process arrives in the ready queue. 
Finish Time :  When process completes its execution and it exits from a system.
Dispatch Latency :  Time required to perform its task by dispatcher is latency time(dispatch latency).
 Completion Time : Time at which the process complete the execution. 
 Turnaround Time :  Total time required by for the process to complete its execution.
                                    Turn Around Time = Completion Time - Arrival Time.
 Burst Time : Time required to complete process execution.
 Waiting Time :: Time spent in ready queue by the process is called as waiting time.
                             Waiting Time = Turnaround time - Burst Time  
 Response Time :: Time taken by the process to generate it's first response when it  receives the request.

​​​​​​​Scheduling algorithms consider above points as a scheduling criteria.
​​​​​​​CPU Scheduling Algorithms 
The Operating System has a major function of deciding the order in which processes / tasks will have access to the processor and the amount of processing time each of these processes or tasks will have. This function of the operating system is termed as process scheduling/ CPU scheduling.
CPU Scheduling is a process of determining which process will use CPU for execution while another process is on hold. The main concept behind CPU scheduling is to make sure that CPU remains busy and dose not  remain idle. Process allocated for execution will be selected by the CPU scheduler. It selects one of the processes in memory that is ready for execution.
Pre-Emptive Scheduling 
In Preemptive Scheduling, the tasks are mostly assigned with their priorities. Sometimes it is important to run a task with a higher priority before another lower priority task, even if the lower priority task is still running. The lower priority task is kept on hold for some time and it resumes when the higher priority task finishes its execution. In this type of scheduling , it is very important that system keeps record of current status of each running process. Context switching is required. It requires a special hardware (for example, a timer) .
Non-Preemptive Scheduling 
 In this type of scheduling method, the CPU is allocated to a specific process. The process that keeps the CPU busy will release the CPU either by context switching or when the process terminates.
Priority Based Scheduling 
Priority scheduling is a method of scheduling processes based on priority. In this method, the scheduler selects the tasks to work as per the priority. Priority scheduling also helps OS to involve priority assignments. The processes with higher priority should be carried out first, whereas jobs with equal priorities are carried out on a round-robin or FCFS basis. Priority can be decided based on memory requirements, time requirements, etc.
Scheduling Criteria  
Scheduling algorithm tries to maximize and minimize the following

​​​​​​​ ​
​​​​​​​Hence, CPU Utilization, Throughput, Turnaround Time, Waiting Time and Response Time are criteria for CPU Scheduling.
Concept of Starvation  
 In case of preemptive algorithms, the processes with larger burst time is constantly kept waiting for CPU , if processes with smaller burst time keep arriving in the queue. Process with higher burst time keeps on waiting for CPU. This is called as starvation. All the processes which depend on starved process also go in the wait state. So if the process has a very high burst time, then it  will possibly be left unexecuted.

To avoide this situation of starvation, the priority of a starved process is increased by an OS so that , process gets CPU for execution. This method of increasing priority is called as is called as Aging. Some standard algorithms are implemented for scheduling. These algorithms are implemented depending on the need and requirement of the system.

Reasons for using a scheduling algorithm 
  • The CPU uses scheduling to improve its efficiency.
  • It helps you to allocate resources among competing processes.
  • The maximum utilization of CPU can be obtained with multi-programming.
  • The processes which are to be executed are in ready queue.

Process Scheduling Algorithms
Reasons for using a scheduling algorithm 
  • The CPU uses scheduling to improve its efficiency.
  • It helps you to allocate resources among competing processes.
  • The maximum utilization of CPU can be obtained with multi-programming.
  • The processes which are to be executed are in ready queue.
Following are the algorithms  
  • First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling
  • Shortest-Job-First (SJF) Scheduling
  • Priority Scheduling
  • Round Robin(RR) Scheduling
Let us discuss these algorithms in details....
1. First Come First Served  
Mode : Non-Preemptive
Criterion : Arrival Time
FCFS also termed as First-In-First-Out i.e. allocate the CPU in the order which the process arrives. When the CPU is free, the process, which is occupying  front of the queue is processesed. Once this process is completed, its PCB is removed from the queue. This scheduling method can be managed with a FIFO queue. It is non-preemptive algorithm, hence process proirity dose not matter.  Jobs are always executed on a first-come, first-served basis.
Advantages of FCFS method  
  • It is easy to implement and use.
  • Every process will be executed.
  • There is no starvation.
Disadvantages 
  • There is no option for pre-emption of a process.
  • This method is poor in performance, and the general wait time for the process to get executed is quite high.
  • Smaller processes stay waiting till larger process completes its execution.
  • If a process is started, then CPU executes the process until it ends.
  • Because there is no pre-emption, if a process executes for a long time, the processes in the back of the queue will have to wait for a long time before they get a chance to be executed.
  • Throughput is low.

Example using FCFS
Process No.    AT  BT   CT  TAT  WT
        P1     0   2    2    2   0
        P2     1   2    4    3   1
        P3     5   3    8    3   0
        P4     6   4   14    6   2

Avg WT=(0+1+0+2)/4
2.  Shortest Job First(SJF)      
This algorithm will always pick the job which is smallest in the ready queue. This algorithm works in two modes, preemptive and non preemptive mode. Algorithm is refered to as STF when it works in  preemptive mode, else it will be refered to as a SRT i.e shortest remaining time first. 
Mode : Non-Preemptive
Criterion : Burst Time  
It is also known as SJF(shortest job first) non- preemptive scheduling. In this method, the process  which has a smallest burst time will be allocated to the CPU. Since this is non preemptive algorithm, CPU will execute entire process till the end and then it will switch to the next process. This method is mostly applied in batch environments where short jobs are required to be given preferences. This is not an ideal method to implement it in a shared system where the required CPU time is unknown. Process will be preempted only when it is completed.
Advantages of SJF Non-Preemptive scheduling method  
  • Shortest jobs will complete fast.
  • Throughput of  the  system goes high since number of processes completed by CPU in a give time unit increases .
Disadvantage of SJF Non-Pre-emptive scheduling method  
  • If processes of smaller burst time keep on arriving in the ready queue , starvation may occur.
 
3. Shortest remaining time first(SRT)  
Mode :  Preemptive  
Criterion : Burst Time  
In this case , every time , when a new process enters the ready queue, it's burst time is always compared with the remaining execution time of running process. CPU will execute the process with shortest burst time. If currently running process has a smaller burst time, then the same process will execute further. Else this process will be pre-empted and a newly entered process will be taken for execution.
Advantages of SJF Preemptive scheduling method  
  • Smaller processes will execute first.
  • Throughput will be high.
Disadvantage of SJF Pre-emptive scheduling method  
  • If processes of smaller burst time keep on arriving in the ready queue , starvation may occur.
  • Context switching between the processes increases the overhead on the system.

Problems on FCFC  and  SJF                                                                                                                                                        Following is a Gantt chart showing how proesses executes using FCFS and SRT algorithm .

4. Round-Robin Scheduling  (RR)
Mode :  Pre-emptive
Criterion :  Time Quantum
Round robin is the oldest, simplest scheduling algorithm. The name of this algorithm comes from the round-robin principle, where each person gets an equal share of something in turn. It is mostly used for scheduling algorithms in multitasking. This algorithm method helps for starvation free execution of processes.
Round robin is a model which is clock-driven. Time slice should be minimum, which is assigned for a specific task to be processed. However, it may vary for different processes.
Advantages of Round-Robin Scheduling  
  • Every process will be executed.
  • No starvation.
  • Very high throughput.
Disadvantage of Round-Robin Scheduling 
  • This method requires additional hardware called as Timer.
  • Context switching adds overhead to the system.

Problem on RR

5. Priority Algorithm  
Starvation is  one of the major problem in some algorithms, hence the concept of assigning a priority to the process was introduced in process scheduling algorithms. Here every process was given a priority, and now process execution was on priority basis. In priority scheduling in algorithm, processes are executed on the basis of their priority. The jobs / processes with higher priority are executed first.  Priority is given to the process at the time of process creation, and its entry is done in PCB i.e process control block.
​​​​​​​ 
Priority of processes depends on some factors such as 
  • Time limit
  • Memory requirements of the process
  • Ratio of average I/O to average CPU burst time   
  • There can be more factors on the basis of which priority of a process / job is determined.
Priority to the process is assigned by the scheduler. These priorities of processes are represented as simple integers in a fixed range such as 0 to 7, or maybe 0 to 4095. These numbers depend on the type of the systems.

Multilevel scheduling algorithms
 It may happen that processes in the ready queue can be divided into different classes where each class has its own scheduling needs.
For example,
A common division is made between foreground(or interactive) processes and background (or batch) processes. These two types of processes have different response-time requirements, and so might have different scheduling needs. In addition, foreground processes may have priority over background processes.
               
​​​​​​​A multi-level queue scheduling algorithm partitions the ready queue into several separate queues. The processes are permanently assigned to one queue, generally based on some property of the process, such as memory size, process priority, or process type. Each queue has its own scheduling algorithm. The foreground queue might be scheduled by the Round Robin algorithm, while the background queue is scheduled by an FCFS algorithm.
Characteristic of Multiple-Level Queues Scheduling 
  • Multiple queues need to be maintained for processes with some characteristics.
  • Every queue may have its separate scheduling algorithms.
  • Priorities are given for each queue.
Interprocess communication
Inter Process Communication (IPC)    
 A process can be of two types:
  • Independent process.
  • Co-operating process.
An independent process is independent and  is not affected by other process. While a co-operating process can be affected by other  executing processes. Inter-process communication (IPC) is a mechanism that allows processes to communicate with each other and synchronize their actions.
Processes can communicate with each other through
  •  Shared Memory
  •  Message passing
Figure  below shows a basic structure of communication between processes via the shared memory method and via the message passing method.

​
Communication using shared memory  
Whenever the memory is shared by the processes it uses some shared variable and implementation of it depends on the programmer.
A processes can use shared memory for extracting information as a record from another process as well as for delivering any specific information to other processes. Example of Consumer - Producer (Bounded Buffer) which we have studied earlier follows the same concept of sharing memory. Here producer and consumer use same memory which is a shared memory. Both producer process and consumer process will work in sync with each other and will communicate with each other via shared resource which is a memory in this case.
Communication using message passing  
In this method, processes communicate with each other without using any kind of shared memory. If two processes p1 and p2 want to communicate with each other, they proceed as follows:
  1. Establish a communication link (if a link already exists, no need to establish it again).
  2. Start exchanging messages using basic primitives.
We need at least two primitives:
  •   send(message, destination) or send(message)
  •   receive(message, host) or receive(message)

​
The message size can be of fixed size or of variable size. If it is of fixed size, it is easy for an OS designer but complicated for a programmer and if it is of variable size then it is easy for a programmer but complicated for the OS designer. Shared memory is created in the kernel part of memory. System calls such as send and receive are used for communication.
A standard message can have two parts , header and body.   
Header
The header part is used for storing message type, destination id, source id, message length, and control information.
​​​​​​​The control information contains information like what to do if system runs out of buffer space, sequence number, priority. Generally, message is sent using FIFO style.
Advantage 
  •      Less error prone.
  •      Message is sent explicitely to the desired user.
Disadvantage 
  •      Little slower
  •      Marshalling/Unmarshalling  of information is required for each mesage sent.
( Marshalling: the act of taking a collection of data items (platform dependent) and assembling them into the external data representation (platform independent).
  Unmarshalling: the process of disassembling data that is in external data representation form, into a locally interpretable form.)
Message Passing through Communication Link  
 A link has some capacity that determines the number of messages that can reside in it temporarily. Every link   has a queue associated with it which can be of zero capacity, bounded capacity, or unbounded capacity. In zero capacity, the sender waits until the receiver informs the sender that it has received the message. In non-zero capacity cases, a process does not know whether a message has been received or not after the send operation. For this, the sender must communicate with the receiver explicitly. Implementation of the link depends on the situation, it can be either a direct communication link or an in-directed communication link.
Direct Communication 
Here links are implemented when the processes use a specific process identifier for the communication, but it is hard to identify the sender ahead of time.
e.g  print server.
  
In-direct Communication 
In Indirect message passing, processes use mailboxes (also referred to as ports) for sending and receiving the messages. Each mailbox has a unique id and processes can communicate only if they share a mailbox. Link is established only if processes share a common mailbox and a single link can be associated with many processes.  Each pair of processes can share several communication links and these links may be unidirectional or bi-directional.
Message Passing through Exchanging the Messages 
Message passing is done by Synchronous or Asynchronous method. Sometimes process waits for some event, such as resource becoming available or completion of an I/O operation. In this case , process is blocked till another event is completed.  IPC is possible between the processes on same computer as well as on the processes running on different computer i.e. in network/distributed system. In both cases, the process may or may not be blocked while sending a message or attempting to receive a message. Hence, message passing may be of blocking or non-blocking type.
Synchronous Message Passing  
Blocking is considered synchronous message passing. Here there are two terminologies
1. Blocking Send  
     In this case, sender will be blocked until the message is received by receiver.
2. Blocking Receiver 
     In this case receiver will be blocked  until a message is available.
Asynchronous Message Passing 
Non-blocking is considered asynchronous message passing.
1. Non-blocking Send
     Here the sender sends the message and continues.
2. Non-blocking Receive
     Here the receiver receives a valid message or null.

Hence we can say that, for a sender it is more natural to be non-blocking after message passing as there may be a need to send the message to different processes. However, the sender expects acknowledgment from the receiver in case the send fails. Similarly, it is more natural for a receiver to be blocking after issuing the receive as the information from the received message may be used for further execution. At the same time, if the message sent keep on failing, the receiver will have to wait indefinitely. That is why we also consider the other possibility of message passing. 
​​​​​​​
Examples of IPC systems  
Posix : uses shared memory method.
Mach : uses message passing
Windows XP : uses message passing using local procedural calls
Communication in client/server Architecture:
Pipe
Socket
Remote Procedural calls (RPCs)

Threads Concept
  • A thread is a path of execution within a process.
  • A process can contain multiple threads.
  • Thread is an execution unit which consists of its own program counter, a stack, and a set of registers.
  • Threads are also known as Lightweight Processes.
  • Each thread belongs to exactly one process and no thread can exist outside a process.
  • Each thread represents a separate flow of control
​

The idea is to achieve parallelism by dividing a process into multiple threads.
For example, in a browser, multiple tabs can be different threads.
MS Word uses multiple threads: one thread to format the text, another thread to process inputs, etc.
Advantages of threads 
1. Responsiveness
   If the process is divided into multiple threads, if one thread completes its execution, then its output can be immediately returned.
2. Faster context switch
    Context switch time between threads is lower compared to process context switch. Process  context  switching requires more overhead on OS as well as CPU.
3. Effective utilization of multiprocessor system
    If we have multiple threads in a single process, then we can schedule multiple threads on multiple processor. This will make process execution faster.   
4. Resource sharing 
   Resources like code, data, and files can be shared among all threads within a process.
Note: Stack and registers cannot be shared among the threads.
           Each thread has its own stack and  registers.
5. Communication 
    Communication between multiple threads is easier, as the threads share common address space, while in process we have to follow some specific communication technique for communication between two processes.

Threads are implemented in following two ways....
User Level Threads     --  User managed threads
Kernel Level Threads  --  Operating System managed threads acting on kernel, an operating system core.
User level thread 
                In this case, application manages thread management. kernel is not aware of the existence of threads. The thread library contains code for creating and destroying threads, for passing message and data between threads, for scheduling thread execution and for saving.Thread switching does not require Kernel mode privileges. User level thread can run on any operating system. Scheduling can be application specific in the user level thread. User level threads are fast to create and manage. Management of user level thread is simple.,It means creating threads, switching and synchronization between threads is easy.
   
Kernel Level Threads 
In this case, thread management is done by the Kernel.
There is no thread management code in the application area.
Kernel threads are supported directly by the OS.
Kernel threads are generally slower to create and manage.
Difference between Thread and Process        
Process Thread
Process is heavy weight or resource intensive.Thread is light weight taking lesser resources than the  process.
Process switching needs interaction with operating
system. Hence increasing system overhead .		Thread switching does not need to interact with OS.
Context switching in process needs system interaction.Context Switching in threads is comparatively easier then process.
Process contains its different code and data.Threads of same process share code but maintain heir individual stack and registers. 
Types Of Threads 
Any application can be programmed to be multithreaded.    
Multithreading models are of three types.
1. Many to Many  
​

In this model, many user level threads multiplexes to the Kernel thread of smaller or equal numbers.
The number of Kernel threads may be specific to either a particular application or a particular machine.

In this model, developers can create as many user threads as necessary and the corresponding
Kernel threads can run in parallels on a multiprocessor.

2. Many to one 
​
Maps many user level threads to one Kernel level thread.
Thread management is done in user space.
When thread makes a blocking system call, the entire process will be blocked.
Only one thread can access the Kernel at a time, so multiple threads are unable to run in parallel on
multiprocessors.

3. One to one 
​

There is one to one relationship of user level thread to the kernel level thread.
This model provides more concurrency than the many to one model.
It also allows another thread to run when a thread makes a blocking system call.
It supports multiple thread to execute in parallel on microprocessors.
Most widely used.
 
Multithreaded Programming

​

A multi-threaded program contains two or more parts that can run concurrently and each part can handle a different task at the same time making optimal use of the available resources specially when your computer has multiple CPUs. Multi-threading enables us to write in a way where multiple activities can proceed concurrently in the same program.

The extremely fast processing speed of today's microprocessors make multithreading possible. Even though the processor executes only one instruction at a time, threads from multiple programs are executed so fast that it appears multiple programs are executing concurrently.        

Each CPU cycle executes a single thread that links to all other threads in its stream. This synchronization process occurs so quickly that it appears all the streams are executing at the same time. This can be described as a multithreaded program, as it can execute many threads while processing.

​​​​​​​ Each thread contains information about how it relates to the overall program. While in the asynchronous processing stream, some threads are executed while others wait for their turn. Multithreading requires programmers to pay careful attention to prevent race conditions and deadlocks.
